gold_caption: You aim your bishop at f7, the weak spot near their king. A fine attacking spot, though the engine liked pushing d4 to grab more center. Lesson: in open games, taking the center with d4 is often even stronger than a quick bishop move.
You retreat the bishop to g3, the best square, eyeing their weak dark squares. Calm and correct.
Qe2 is okay, but d4 was stronger to open the middle while you have the two bishops. Lesson: when you own the bishop pair, opening the position makes them even better.
You play Bxa6, smashing the pawn cover in front of their king. Perfect — this opens the b-file for a deadly attack.
They guard the pawn with d6 instead of the more active Nc6. This is a quiet, slightly passive setup — you have free time to build the center with d4.
Their knight leaps to d4, a strong central post. Meet it with Be3 to develop and contest the squares.
Qf5+ checks, but Qh5+ was sharper to harass the king. Still, you keep their king walking.
Nd5 is okay but f4 (activating your side) was sharper. Your knight does jump to a strong central spot though.
Rf3+ gives a check. Quietly building with b3 was a hair better, but the check still pesters their king.
Qe4+ checks and centralizes with power. Good, top choice.
e5+ gives a check with your pawn and offers a queen trade. Good — this is the engine's top move.
They develop their knight and eye your e4 pawn. Keep an eye on that pawn.
They put the bishop on the long line aiming at your king side. Watch that bishop's aim at g2 later.
They recapture with the bishop. You have a strong attack brewing on f7.
You trade bishops. Right idea — fewer pieces means your extra material wins easier.
You step the king to d2, the best square. Stay very alert; your king is in the open.
They check and grab your c3 pawn. Your king is getting chased — stay accurate.
They calmly block with the king to h7. Now their attack is real — you must defend with great care.
Rg4# ends the game. You played a brilliant winning game until your king got caught in the open — the big lesson is to keep your king safe before chasing more material.
Good — your knight develops and eyes the center. You are right on plan.
Good — you slide the bishop back and keep it safe and useful. Exactly right.
Strong — g4 kicks White's knight and keeps your attack rolling. Well done.
Good — you accept the trade on great terms. Simple and correct.
He blocks with Be2. Calm and safe. Keep developing — bring out your knight with Nc6.
He castled, getting his king safe. Normal. You keep building — your pieces are well placed.
He took with Nxd4, the right move. Now take back with the pawn, exd4, to keep things tidy.
He played Bg3, retreating the bishop. This is loose — you can strike with f5, gaining space and rolling your pawns forward.
He played Nc5, hopping the knight back to safety. Calm position. Keep your pieces active and look for pawn pushes.
He played Rb3 instead of trading rooks. A small slip. Bring your rook to a5 to stay active and pressure him.
Black pushes the f-pawn and weakens the king. This is a small mistake. The clean reply was d4 to open the center and use Black's loose position.
Black takes your f5 pawn back. That's fair — pieces are roughly even now, so just keep developing.
a5 attacks the bishop, but Bxc6 was still the strong winning move. Lesson: keep looking for that same idea until it's gone.
Perfect. Bxc6 grabs the knight, your best move. You keep the material fair.
b3 is too quiet and lets Black grab your c2 pawn. Better was Qe7 to make threats. Lesson: when ahead, stay active, don't sit back.
You missed Qe5. Rc1 is okay but the strong central queen move was much better. Lesson: a queen in the middle does the most.
Qd7 is okay but Rc6 was stronger to crash in. Small slip, you're still winning big.
You bring out your knight and attack the e4 pawn. This is the engine's top move too — well done developing with a threat.

This knight jump looks active but it loses a lot — the knight gets chased and does nothing. Much better was Nc6, simple development. Lesson: don't move one piece many times in the opening; bring everyone out first.
You take the rook with check — the right follow-up, winning the exchange. Good, you are up a little material now.
You develop the knight, which is okay, but taking the bishop on c4 first was stronger and free of trouble. Lesson: grab good trades when offered before doing other things.
Big blunder by him — Qc2 leaves the h3 pawn loose. Punish it right now with Nxh3+, winning material with check! Lesson: always look for knight checks near the king.
He trades rooks. Recapture and stay solid.
His queen comes to e3 to stay active. Drive it back and invade with Qd1.
He shuffles his king back; his pieces are still tangled. Repeat the check — Qc2+ keeps poking him.
He pushes e5 trying to make threats. Smash through — take the knight with Rxf3 and start trading down to victory.
He checks from e8 instead of grabbing your pawn — a slip that helps you. Block or step away with Kc7 and stay calm.
He checks to slow you down. Just step your king to safety and keep your winning plan.
He plays Nc3 to attack your queen and gain time. You must move the queen to safety.
He plays Bc4 to aim his bishop at your f7 square. Block that bishop with e6.
He plays Ne4 — a blunder! His knight just walks into trouble. Take it with Nxe4 and you win material.
He must take back with Qxf3. Now grab the free rook in the corner with Qxa1!
He plays Rad1 — a slip. His f3 pawn is weak: swing your rook with Rf5 to win it.
He takes with fxg4. Think before you recapture.
He trades with Bxf4+ (check). Take back with your rook.
He plays a4 — a blunder! Play f4+ (check): after his king moves, fxe3+ wins his rook.
White takes back, and now the center is open. Keep getting your pieces out.
White develops the knight. Just keep finishing your development.
Big mistake by White — castling here drops a piece. Punish it: play Bxh4 and after Nxh4 you grab another piece with Nxc3.
White pushes the h-pawn to chase your queen again. Retreat it calmly.
You give a knight check. Best move — it gains time.

This is the big one — Neg4 hangs your queen, and White just takes it with Qxc5. The simple Qc6+ check was winning. Lesson: before moving, always ask 'is my queen safe?' — check every capture your opponent has.
You take back with the pawn. Best move.
You step the king to h7 — the right square. Best move.
You castle and tuck your king safe in the corner. Smart and timely.
You bring out your last knight to develop. Fine, though b4 was even stronger to attack the bishop and gain space.
You play a4 to gain space on the queenside. Fine, though the big center punch d4 was the most powerful.
Black takes back on d6 and offers a queen trade. Trading queens is fine since you are far ahead — Qxd6 keeps it simple.
You grab the a5 pawn, but it pulls your knight away and lets Black get active. Be3 was safer to keep your pieces working together. Lesson: don't chase pawns when your pieces are doing important jobs.
Black plays g4 to open lines at your king. Be careful now — meet it firmly, the calm h4 holds things.
Black moves the king to g7. Now promote — a8=Q makes a brand new queen.
White plays e4 and grabs the center. This is the most common first move, so just develop your pieces calmly.
White plays h3 to make luft for the king. Now is a good moment to grab that e3 bishop.
White plays e4 to kick your queen. Just move the queen to a safe, active square.
White plays Nbd2 to bring the knight toward e4. You can keep building your pressure on the center.
White plays Rae1 to pile up on the e-file. Watch the e5 pawn and keep your pieces defended.
White plays a4, a slow pawn move that drifts. Now is the moment to grab the file with Raf8.
White takes the queen with gxh3, going up a lot of material. You must grab whatever you can back right away.
White grabs the e5 pawn with Nxe5 — but this allows a check. Hit back with Rg5+.
White takes with axb5. Recapture and keep things tidy.
White plays Nxg5+, winning your rook with check. You must recapture.
They defend the pawn with d6, but it is a bit passive. They blocked their own dark bishop. You are doing fine.
Your knight jumps to the rim to chase the queen, but recapturing on c4 was simpler and kept things equal. Lesson: a knight on the edge of the board is often weak.
They make luft (air) for their king with h6. Quiet move. Just keep building with Be3.
Their knight comes to c5 to block. Trade it off with your bishop — Bxc5 is the clean reply.
They develop the knight to e7. Now push a5 to crack open their king's shelter.
Their king runs to b7 into the open. Now Nb5 sets up a deadly net around the king.
Huge blunder — the king steps to b7 and walks into a forced mate. Play Qa7+ and it is checkmate in two.
They push d4 to challenge the center. This trades pawns; you can just take it.
They push e5 and now your f6 knight is attacked and must run. This was their strong plan from the c3 move — your center is falling apart.
They play Qf4, lining the queen up to strike at f7. You are one move from disaster — castling (O-O) was urgent to save the king.
Black brings out a knight and attacks your e5 pawn. Just keep it defended.
Black pushes again to chase your bishop. Move it to safety on b3.
Black weakened his king with g6. You can jump in with Qf6, putting your queen on a strong, annoying square.
Black blundered. Play cxd5 — after the trades you win a piece because his pieces get overloaded on d5.
Black's bishop now aims down the long line at your center. Remember: pushing your king pawn to e5 to gain space was a strong idea here.
Black pushes a pawn that doesn't really threaten you. You stay comfortable with more space.
Black develops and looks at your e5 pawn. Keep that pawn defended.
Black grabs your b2 pawn with the queen — but it's deep in your camp. Trap it: Rab1 hits the queen.
Black's bishop attacks your rook. Move it to safety.
Black wins your side pawn back with the bishop. You're still up a lot of material.
Black's bishop shuffles. You can simply grab the a6 pawn with Rxa6.
White plays g3 to fanchetto the bishop, but this lets you take charge. You can push d4 here and gain a strong space advantage.
You develop with Nf6. You missed Nb4, which was much stronger and would have given you a big advantage. Lesson: look for active knight jumps before quiet development.
You play Ng4 to attack. The quiet c6 was better; Ng4 lets some of your edge slip.
White recaptures on e2 with the knight. The dust settles — count your pieces and plan.
White plays a3 to gain space on the side. Stay active — your pieces are better.
White grabs the pawn with Rxf7+, check. Block or step the king away and stay calm — you're still fine.
White takes the e5 pawn with the bishop. Material is roughly even — play actively.
White plays Ncd3 to centralize the knight. Keep your rook active.
You play Rxe3+, the best move, a check that wins a pawn.
You play Kc7, the best move, still hunting the knight.
You play Rg1, but Rg3 was better to support the pawn.
You push g4, but Ra2 was much stronger to grab pawns.
You play Kf5, but Kd6 was safer. Try to keep your king close to the action.
You play Rxa6, the best move, winning the bishop. Now you're ahead.
You play Ra8. Almost equal to the engine's Ra1 — a fine, safe rook move.
White develops a knight. Nothing to fear — keep developing.
A slow pawn move that does not help White. Punish it by developing — Bc5 puts your bishop on a strong diagonal.
White trades his strong knight for your bishop — a gift that lets you off the hook. Just take back.
Too greedy — this grabs a side pawn but your queen gets trapped in the corner after Rb1. Qxe4 took a safe central pawn instead. Lesson: don't chase pawns into the corner with your queen.
This lets White hit your bishop with Nd3 and later wreck your kingside with Bxf6. Bf8 first kept everything solid. Lesson: tuck loose pieces to safety before grabbing pawns.
Taking back opens your own king, and the f6 pawn falls to Bxf6 anyway. The active Qd2 made more trouble. Lesson: when behind, look for counterplay instead of sad recaptures.
The king walks forward. Okay, though Kg8 tucked it safer.
You retreat the queen but miss Nxe5, which wins the strong bishop. Lesson: look for captures before quiet retreats.
You grab some space on the side. Okay, but getting the rook active with Re6 was better.
Black copies you and plays e5. This is a very normal answer, and now you have a balanced game.
Black pushes the pawn to e4 to chase your other knight. Hop it back to d4 where it is safe.
You develop the bishop to f4. Not bad, but dxe4 was again the cleaner way to win the pawn and stay safe.
You take the knight with Nxd4. Good clean trade.
You play Qf3, but this is a serious slip. Bxd6 first removed the dangerous bishop; now Black gets a strong attack on your king.
Black plays Qd2 and it is checkmate. The lesson: when you are far ahead, trade pieces and keep your king safe instead of grabbing pawns.
You build a safe house for the queen and open a path for your bishop — solid.

Pinning the knight looks active, but here a pawn just kicks the bishop and it gets traded. Qc7 was better — tuck the queen safe and get ready to castle. Lesson: don't put a bishop where a pawn can chase it.
Recapturing with the knight leaves your g7 pawn open to Bxg7. Kxd7 was better and kept the pawn safe.
You bring the knight to g6, a safe and useful square. Good fix.
You recapture with the other rook — just as good. Material is even again.
The king steps out, but a6 first made a safe pocket and slowed White down. Lesson: before moving the king, give it a safe square to run to.
You walk the king up — okay, but stay very careful of more checks.
Bc5 develops a piece, but d5 was clearly better — it attacks the center and opens lines for your pieces. Lesson: when the center is loose, push a pawn there instead of just developing.
axb4 trades pawns; it's okay, though d5 was a touch better. No real harm done.
Good — Ba7 keeps the bishop safe, and it still aims down the line at White's f2 square.
Checkmate! Your queen lands on f2, protected by the a7-bishop you set up long ago. Beautiful finish — well done!
Black calmly builds with d6 to free his bishop. Nothing scary. Keep developing — bring out your knight and bishop.
Black plays a6 to kick your bishop. Just take the knight with Bxc6 — it gives Black a small weakness.
Black grabs the d5 pawn but this lets you win material! Play Qd4 — it hits the rook on h8 and the bishop can't save everything.
Black recaptures with the queen, forced. You are still way ahead. Keep trading and bring your rooks into play.
Black pushes e5 to block your queen. This opens his king a bit. Give a check with Qg4+ to grab the initiative.
Slip — Re1 wastes time and lets Black get active. Rxc2 was strong, trading and grabbing the b-pawn. Lesson: when ahead, trade pieces and don't drift.
You play Qa7 to offer a queen trade. Fine idea — Qa8 was a touch sharper, but trading queens helps you win. Good.
You play Rb7, putting a rook on the strong 7th rank. Great — rooks love the 7th. Keep squeezing.
You play Rab4 to stop and win the b-pawn. Exactly right — your rooks easily handle his last hope.
Your opponent opens a path for their dark bishop. This is fine for you — keep developing.
Your opponent castles. Good for them, normal for you — just keep building your plan.
Big mistake by your opponent — the knight jump to g4 leaves them much worse. Punish it with e5! This pawn push attacks the f6 knight and gains a strong center.
You give check with Qg4+ — the exact engine move. Your queen joins the attack on the open king.

Rh3 is a serious blunder — it hangs the rook and your opponent can just take it with the bishop. Ne4 was the move, sending the knight in with a strong attack. Lesson: before moving, check if the square is guarded by an enemy piece.
You recapture with cxd3 — the correct move. Your position stays steady.
You take the pawn, but d4 was much stronger. Lesson: when the enemy king is open, hit the center to open lines instead of grabbing a side pawn.
You trade with check. Ng3 was a bit better, but this is okay and simplifies the game.
You block the check and attack the bishop at the same time. Two jobs in one move — well done.
You take the bishop, but Be3 was better. Still, taking a piece is fine.
You take the queen. You are now winning big — just stay careful and trade pieces.
They bring a rook into the game. Stay active and use your bishop.
A rook check. Move your king to a safe square — Kc2 was best.
They double rooks but it was not best. Keep your rook busy and try Rf7 to attack pawns.
A passive rook move; their rooks were stronger staying active. Use this break to push your pawns or check.
Black guards the pawn with a knight. Nothing to fear — keep developing your pieces.
Small slip: Qf3+ lets the win slip. You could have played Qxe5 to simply win a free pawn. Lesson: before checking, ask if a quiet capture wins more.
Bg5 develops the bishop and pins ideas, though pushing a4 first was a bit better.
Nf3 develops, but again Nd5 was the powerful square for your knight. Lesson: a knight on a central hole the enemy can't chase is golden.
Black blunders badly with Bxg4. Now Qxb7 grabs a pawn and attacks, and your threats roll in.
Black blocks with the bishop. Now turn your rooks toward the king.
Rgxf6+ smashes in with check and forces the king's defense apart.
You play e5 to guard the pawn and grab more space. Nice and solid.
Their bishop steps back to c4, aiming at your f7. Bring your queen to e7 to stay solid.
Their bishop goes to f4. A quiet move for you — finish developing with Nd7.
Their bishop retreats to b3. Keep rolling your pawns — c5 next is strong.
They take your knight with Bxf6, but this helps you — just recapture with gxf6.
Their knight reroutes to d2. You can win the d4 pawn — Rxd4 grabs it.
They push b3 to challenge your c4 pawn. You can take, but watch the lines carefully.
Their rook drops back to f1 to defend. Keep your bishop active — Bd3 hits the rook.
They push c6 toward making a queen. Step the bishop back to a6 to slow it down.
Their knight checks on e7 to try a fork. Step the king to g7 and keep your big rooks.
Their Nb6 is a slip. Save your bishop with Bb7 and stay in control.
Their king runs to f2. Now grab the rook on a1 with Rxa1.
You snap off the knight with Rxb7. Now you are up a rook and a knight — just push your pawn home to win. Well played!
Nf3 develops your last minor piece and gets you ready to castle. Smooth and solid.
You recapture with dxe5. Good — you still have a strong pawn on e5.
gxh3 takes the bishop. You are now up a whole piece. Excellent — that is winning material.
Qf3 is the right defense. It guards your pieces and keeps your king safe. Good save.
cxd3 recaptures the knight. Perfect — you got the material back. Stay alert.
Bishop to e2 blocks the check and develops a piece. Calm and strong.
a3 is again too slow and lets your edge slip. d4 was the move — claim the center while you can. Lesson: don't drift on the sides; play in the middle.
Rook to d1 puts a rook on the open file behind your queen. Good teamwork between your pieces.
Nxf6+ — yes! A check that rips open the king and forces their reply. The attack is now winning.
Qh7+ — the queen lands next to the king with check, driving it to its doom.
You block the check with your bishop. Calm and correct.
You bring the knight back to c3. Best square — undo the earlier rim trip.
Black takes back with the pawn. Now you can re-route your knights to strong squares.
Black lifts a rook to b8. They are getting ready to push on the side — stay alert.
Black's queen swings to f5, eyeing your king. Get pieces back to defend and stay calm.
Black plays Bb7, lining the bishop up for mate on the long line. The threat is mate next move and it is very hard to stop.
Black's queen runs back home to d8. You have gained time and a head start in development.
Black develops the knight to f6, a normal good move. Nothing to fear yet — finish your development.
Knight to f3 develops and is a fine, active move. Good.
d3 is passive and gives up the center fight. Push d5 now so you own both center squares.
h4 is another weak pawn push that ignores development. Grab the chance with Bg4 — your bishop comes out with tempo and pressure.
a3 is a small, slow pawn move that does not threaten anything. Continue your plan with Ne7 to finish developing.
Bishop to f4 develops a piece, but Nf3 first was smoother. Small slip, your position is still healthy. Lesson: get knights out early before the bishops.
You take back with the knight. Perfect, now you have both bishops, a small long-term plus.
You push g4 to gain space and chase the h5 bishop. A bit risky near your king, but playable.
Bishop to e3 is fine, but Bg3 kept it on a better diagonal. Very minor, nothing lost.
White builds a big pawn center. Keep developing and plan a pawn break later.
White takes back but now has doubled, weak pawns. These pawns are a target for you.
White develops his last knight. Nothing to fear; finish developing.
White's rook goes to a passive spot. You are better; use your extra pawn.
White's queen comes to hit your corner knight. Keep your queen active and don't panic.
White takes your knight, so you lost that piece. Play simply now and use your remaining pieces.
White's bishop aims at the long line toward your king. Keep an eye on that diagonal.
White's knight attacks your rook on f5. Move it to safety.
You grab the pawn back with your queen. Careful: the queen sits in the open and will get chased around.
You keep the pin by sliding back to h5. But this lets them push you around — trading on f3 was simpler.
You recapture and open the h-file for your rook. Good.
You move the queen to safety, but c5 gave you more active play. A small inaccuracy.
You take the queen with check. Excellent — you win the trade.
This is a mistake — you should have taken the knight with Nxe4. Why: now their knight jumps to g5 and attacks your weak e6 pawn.
You recapture the knight. The position has simplified.
You snatch the f2 pawn with the bishop. Good, you win a pawn.
You take the rook back with check. Fine, though pushing g5 first was a touch stronger.
You centralize your king. Good — the king is a strong piece in the endgame.
You push the e-pawn forward. Great — this passer is your hope.
You bring the king back, almost as good as pushing. Fine.
This is the game-losing move — your king walks into trouble and your pawn falls. Kf4 was needed. Lesson: in a race, keep your king close to your pawn and away from checks.
You push the pawn to the 7th rank. Good — it is one step from queening.
You head toward your pawn with Kf2. Good — trying to queen.
You take the bishop back. A fair trade, but you are losing.
He takes back with his knight. Now his knight sits in the middle.
Lucky break — he missed g4, which would have won your knight! Now play g6 to give your knight a safe home.
He castles his king to safety. You should think about castling too.
He gives back the advantage instead of trapping your queen. Slide your queen to safety with Qc7.
He offers to trade queens. You can avoid it or accept; both are okay.
He takes your rook, winning the exchange. You are down material now — play actively to make trouble.
He grabs your pawn but loses some ground. Take back with your bishop.
He takes your queen with his bishop. Take the bishop back.
Black plays e6, opening a path for the dark bishop. This is calm; just keep developing.
Black plays Nxc4, taking your bishop. You're down more now. Keep your king safe and don't panic — Qe2 was the steady reply.
Black plays Nc4 to save the knight — but this is a slip for Black. You can play Qb5! hitting the knight and getting active, winning back ground.
Black plays Ne4, a strong jump toward your king. Be careful: meet threats calmly, Qb4 keeps your queen active.
Black plays Nxe3+, taking your queen with check. The game is basically lost now. Don't be sad — the big takeaway is to always check for knight forks and checks before each move.
Be2 is a slow bishop move. This was your chance — push d5 to hit the center hard.
Bxf6 trades bishop for knight and breaks the pin. Now you must recapture.
O-O puts your opponent's king in the corner — but it walked into your plan. The f4 jump is now very strong, so go Nf4.
Rf1 defends the f2 spot. Keep the pressure; Nf4 was the clean way to keep squeezing.
Qc5+ gives a check but lets the queen be pushed back. Just step away with Kb8 and you're fine.
Nxe5 recaptures. Defend carefully; activate your rooks and watch the passed pawns.
Ne5 attacks your rook and forks ideas. Just slide the rook to safety with Re7.
Kh2 just tidies the king. You have time — bring your king up or grab pawns.
h4 starts pushing the h-pawn — that is the dangerous passed pawn. Double your rooks with Rce2 to stop it and attack.
Rxh7 grabs another pawn, but it let your rook get active. Use Rg4 to attack and hold the passed pawns back.
Rh7+ checks again. Simply step the king; both corners are okay.
Kh3 walks the king toward its own pawns. Race your b-pawn and bring your king to help.
Kh4 marches their king up to help the pawns. Keep pushing b and keep your rook ready to block.
Kxg6 takes your rook. Now you only have the pawn — promote it and try to give checks.
Kg7 guards the h-pawn. Keep maneuvering your queen to win it or force the king away.
Kf8 steps out. Keep your checks safe and circle the pawn.
Kg8 hides again. Keep checks coming and start advancing your king.
Kh8 is forced into the corner. Use this moment to bring your king closer.
The opponent pushed a side pawn to a5. This does nothing useful, so just keep building your pieces calmly.
They make room for their dark bishop. A quiet, solid move from them.
They move a rook to d8. Again you have the chance to play the strong e5 push.
They take your rook back. This is part of the trade you wanted.
They push a4 to chase your bishop again. Keep it safe one more step.
Blunder by them with Na5. Punish it right away with Bxd5, winning the pawn and getting a great bishop.
They put the queen on e7. A quiet move; keep improving your pieces.
You take the b5 pawn back to win some material. A good, solid move to fight on.
Black takes your pawn. You can win it back; just recapture in good order.
Black blocks the check with his bishop. The danger is over; you are up a piece.
Black swings his bishop out. A touch loose; Bd6 was better for him. You are fine.
Black's queen steps out to a central square. No immediate danger; keep your pieces working together.
Black takes back with the queen. Even trade; play on.
Black pushes the pawn and attacks your knight. You need to deal with this threat carefully.
Black pushes a pawn, but this loses it — take it with bxa5! Free pawn for you.
Black moves the queen back again. Keep looking at the loose a-pawn you can win.
You develop the knight to f6. Good and natural, but a6 (gaining queenside space) was the top choice here.
You play b5, gaining space on the queenside. This is the best move and pushes the white bishop back. Lesson: b5 grabs room and bothers the c4 bishop.
Your opponent opens with the queen pawn. This is a calm start. Just build your pieces in the middle too.
White trades pawns in the middle. Simple — just take back and stay equal.

Bishop to d6 develops, but the knight on d5 is still annoying. Nf6 was stronger because it challenges that knight and dares White to trade. Lesson: when an enemy piece is strong in your center, look for a move that attacks it.
You snap up the queen with cxd6. Perfect — you spotted the free queen and now you are winning. Lesson: always check if a capture can just be taken back.
Knight to g4 runs to a bad square where it gets chased. Better was Nd5, a calm strong home in the middle. Lesson: when chased, pick a safe square, not a far one.
White gives a check with the bishop. Just block it.
White's queen steps back.
White develops the last knight.
White's knight leaps to g5 and now eyes a deadly Qxh7. You MUST play h6 right now to kick the knight away.
Your opponent copies you. Now you have a classic open game where both sides fight for the center.
They make a small luft and prepare to push d5. Solid by them — keep your pieces ready.
They poke your bishop with the h-pawn. Smart move — now retreat to a safe spot like Be3, not h4.
They line up queen and bishop aiming at your kingside. Stay alert — adding defenders and trading their attackers (like Bxf6) keeps you safe.
Black puts the bishop on b7, aiming at your e4 pawn. Make sure e4 stays protected as you continue.
Knight to g5 was a mistake — it attacks nothing real and wastes time. Simply castling (O-O) was much better and safer. Lesson: don't push a knight forward unless it makes a real threat.
You develop the other knight to f3. Fine, though the small move h3 (to stop a knight coming to g4) was a touch cleaner.
Knight to b3 was off-target; the knight to c4, jumping into the strong central hole, was clearly better. Lesson: send knights toward weak squares in the enemy camp.
Queen to g3 keeps an eye on the kingside. Okay, but f4, breaking open the center, was the more active choice.
Bishop to f1 was passive and lost ground; the knight to d4 to fight back in the center was better. Lesson: in trouble, look for active defense, not just retreating.
Black gives a knight check on h3 — you should just take it. Capturing with the bishop is forced and fine.
Black also puts the queen out on f6, blocking their own knight. This helps you — just develop with Nc3 and play normally.
Black blocks with the bishop on d7. Quiet move — you can now reposition your queen or castle soon.
Black lines the rook up on c8. They are slowly improving; you should trade or castle to get safe.
Black's knight returns to c6. Calm position — keep developing and look to castle.
Black recaptures with the pawn. Now you can win the c7 pawn with your queen.
Black blunders with Kf8 instead of Kd8. You can play Qd7 and then snap up the c7 pawn with a great position.
Black plays Qf3 to force trades. Just go along with it — take the knight on e7.
Black blocks the danger with Kg8. Keep improving; bring the rook in with Re1.
Black pushes h5 to run the pawn. Stop it early — the engine likes pushing f6 to make your own passed pawn strong.
Black pushes h3 to make a runner. You can take the d6 pawn with check first.
Black brings the king to e5. Now start marching your own pawns; push your king up too.
Black takes back with the king. Now run your queenside pawns and they will queen.
Black's king chases over, but it's too far away. Keep pushing your pawns.
Black's king comes to c6 to block. Push b7 next to make a new queen.
Nf6 develops a knight and helps guard the center. Quiet and fine.
exd3 wins the bishop. Lesson: when a fork wins material, grab it right away.
Nd3 plants the knight deep, but Ne6 was cleaner. Still, you keep the pressure.
Bd7 blocks the check and keeps everything safe. Correct.
Re8 develops the rook but again leaves the h1 knight to die. Nf2 was urgent.
Nxb2 grabs another pawn. Tiny bit greedy, but fine.
c4 hits the queen but cxd4 was stronger. Still okay.
Rb1+ gives the check. Now his king must run.
Bxd8 blocks the check, the only good move. Fine.
Qe6+ keeps the king on the run. Correct.
Qd7+ checks. Okay, just keep him from settling.
Bf8 blocks the check, the only move. Fine.
Qxd4+ wins the pawn with check. Good, keep grabbing safely.
Bxe7 wins his knight for free. Lesson: always check if a checking piece can simply be captured.
They grab your e4 pawn with Nxe4, but this is a small slip. The safe reply now is Qe2, lining up the queen against their knight.
They blunder with Ne4 — a big slip. You can grab the center and chase the knight with d4, gaining time and space.
They blunder with Kd8, walking their king into danger. You can play d3 to free your bishop and start an attack.
They take with cxd5. Recapture and stay solid; you are doing well now.
They shuffle the rook to f8. Quiet move — keep building with moves like c3 to make your king safer.
They check with Bg4+, but it is harmless. Just step the king to d2.
They jump in with Ne5, but this lets you win their bishop. Play Nxg4 to snap it off!
They retreat the king to c7. You are up a lot of material now — push your extra pawns and trade pieces to win.
You bring your knight out to a natural square. Good developing move.
You guard f7 and block the queen's view, but e4 was much stronger to grab space. Lesson: when the center is yours to take, take it.
You recapture with the bishop, and now it eyes the long diagonal. Best move — remember this bishop, it becomes important later.
You push the pawn, chasing the bishop and getting ready to grab d3. Best move.
You centralized the queen, but your king is still stuck in the middle; O-O was better. Lesson: an uncastled king is your biggest risk — fix it first.
Again the slow piece move; Kf7 was the move. Lesson: when one safe move keeps being best, just play it.
You take the knight with your bishop. Best move — you are up material.
Moving the king to safety is good, but Rxa3 was better — it wins a free pawn. Lesson: grab loose pawns when nothing else is urgent.
White moves his rook and blunders. Punish with Bd4, attacking the rook — you win it with Bxe3+ next.
White plays c3 to block your check and support the d4 pawn. This is solid. Your queen on a5 now has fewer good squares, so think about where she goes next.
You play Qxe5+, taking the pawn back with check. Perfect. Material is even and your queen is active with a tempo.
White moves the king to h1 to step out of the check. Normal and safe. Keep developing and bring your king to safety soon.
White gives a check with Qg4+. Just block or step away calmly; Bd7 covers the check nicely. No danger if you stay calm.
White plays Nf3 to reroute the knight. Now you have a nice idea: take the knight with Bxf3, breaking up the pawns near White's king.
White takes your queen with Qxf3. Queens are off now. Just recapture and play the rook endgame carefully.
White pushes c5, sending the passed pawn forward. This pawn is dangerous, so keep your rook ready to stop or win it. Lesson: a passed pawn must be watched every move.
White plays Rd2, shifting the rook. Stay active. Your bishop and rook can keep making threats while your king marches up.
White plays Kf5, the only good king move. Keep your rook active and bring your king and pawns into play.
White recaptures cxb6, keeping a dangerous passed pawn on b6. Check with your rook to push White's king back and slow the pawn.
White plays a6+, pushing the pawn with check. You must move your king now. Be careful — going to the wrong corner can be deadly.

White plays Ra8 checkmate. The game is over. Don't be sad — you played a strong middlegame and a clever endgame; just remember to ask 'what comes after I capture?' and to keep your king out of the corner. Well fought!

They weaken their king with f5 (c5 was safer). Grab the great central square with Be5.
They take your knight back, and now you are up the exchange (rook for bishop).

King steps up. Nothing scary, keep your rooks active.
They slip with b5 (h5 was better). Reposition your rook with R5d3 and keep pressing.
A check from the pawn. Your king must step over.
Blunder again with Bd6+! This time grab it: Rxd6+, then after cxd6 you play Rxd6+ and win the piece.
Their rook stays busy, but it changes little.
They try to block the pawns. March your king up to help.
Their rook swings behind to slow the pawns. Keep king and pawns working together.
They drift a little (Kd7 was better). Keep pushing the pawns.
Be3 develops your bishop, but Nc3 (bringing out the knight) was a little quicker and better. Try to get knights out early too.
You castle your king to safety — a good idea, though the pin Bg5 was a bit sharper. Still, king safety is never wrong.
You make a small pawn move to e3 to support your pieces — solid.

Bd3 develops, but your e3 pawn still hangs to Qxe3+. Play e4 right now to save it.

d5 pushes the pawn and pokes the e6 bishop. Qe5, going to the center, was a little better.

You retreat the bishop to safety. The right call.
Your knight leaps to a strong central square. Great spot for it.
You give a check with the bishop. Fine and active.
Your bishop jumps to e4 and eyes the f3 knight. Strong move.
You check with the rook and stay active. Good rook play.
Your check is okay, but Be4 first was stronger and kept things solid.
You grab the b2 pawn. Fair try to make your own pawns count.
You take the rook with check. Well spotted, a happy ending to fight on.
Small mistake: you pushed a pawn instead of developing. Bg4 was better because it brings a piece out and pins the knight. Lesson: in the opening, get pieces out before pushing extra pawns.
You put the queen on an active square and guard your stuff. Fine.
Great — you check and seize the open e-file. Strong play.
You double your rooks on the e-file. Fine, but Nd5 was still best.
You win the f3 pawn and keep up the attack. Nice.
You make a safe square for your king. Fine (Kf8 was a touch better).
You win a pawn by taking on d3. Good.
Yes! You take the queen with check and grab the material. You are winning.
White just pushes a pawn; nothing changes, you are winning.
The king now has no escape.
Your knight comes out to a strong central square and guards e5. Good, simple development.
You castle and tuck your king into safety. Always a good idea before you attack.
You push a4, charging your pawns at their king. Perfect follow-up to your plan.
Your knight jumps to h4, heading for their king. It works out, though bishop to e3 first was steadier.
Black defends the pawn with the knight. Normal and good.
Good — you take the pawn with exd5. You are up material now.
Now you play d4. Good — your center is strong and your pieces have room.
g3 lets the attack come. The strong move was Qf3 — it grabbed the lead and hit Black's loose bishop.
Rac1 is okay, but Bf4 was a touch better to trade off Black's strong bishop.
You recapture with hxg3. Good, your king stays okay.
Black blunders again with Rf6. Now Bxb8 truly wins the rook — do not miss it twice!

You push d4 and take a big strong center. Excellent — this is the best move and gives you space.
Lesson: a wide pawn center gives your pieces room to grow.

You push d5 and hit their knight. Perfect — this is the best move and starts your attack on their king.
Lesson: when their king goes to one side, throw your pawns at it.

You tuck your king to h1 instead. This throws away a lot — Nxa7+ first was crushing.
Lesson: when you see a strong check that helps your attack, play it before quiet moves.
You take the rook with Nxd8. Winning material is nice, though taking on e6 first was a bit sharper.

You play Bd4, but this loses a lot because their knight can hit your queen with Nf4. Rad1 to connect your rooks was much better.
Lesson: watch for knight jumps that attack your queen.
They swing the queen to h4. Keep your defense tight; you can check with your rook.
They take back with the king. Trades help you slow down their attack.
He brings out a knight. A normal developing move.
He pushes the pawn to chase your knight, but this is a real mistake. You can play Qa5+ check, and after he blocks you win the e5 pawn for free.
His queen steps away. Now play f5 to lock things up and stay solid.
He attacks your bishop and offers a trade. Save your queen first with Qe7.
He takes your knight. Take back and keep your big lead.
His rook retreats. Keep pressing with your extra material.
He defends the third rank. Keep squeezing.
He takes back with the bishop. Now go win his side pawns — start with Rb3.
He grabs your f-pawn. No problem — keep your strong rook.
His king wanders the wrong way. Bring your own king up with Kf6 to help your pawn.
Still chasing in vain. Keep going.
His king steps back. Keep closing the net with checks and your king.
You bring the knight to c6 to add pressure on d4. Playing e6 first was a touch cleaner, but this is okay.
You put the bishop on g7, pointing across the long line. Good spot for it.
You recapture on f6 with the rook. This is forced and the best you have now.
You play Re8 to pin White's knight to the rook. Good — this is your best try to win the piece back.
You start with the king pawn. A great, strong opening that grabs the center right away.
Good capture. You take cleanly and keep the position simple.
Good — you grab the b5 pawn and get some of your lost material back. Smart recovery.
They place their bishop actively. No threat. Just keep developing and connect your rooks.
Black plays e6. This is calm. You can grab the center with e4 next.
Black plays b6 to fianchetto a bishop. Calm. Keep improving your pieces.
Black plays Be7 instead of Ne7, a slip that loses time. Now d5 or Nd2 grabs the edge.
Black recaptures dxe5. Normal. Now your pieces are more active.
Black recaptures hxg4. Now grab the loose pawn.
Black plays Nh6, another weak move. Now Bxg5 is strong, winning a pawn and keeping the heat on Black's king.
Black plays Kg7, the only square. Keep your pieces active and bring in your knight.
Black plays Kxg6, grabbing your bishop. Now win the f6 pawn with Nxf6 and keep your edge.
Black plays Kh7, the only move. Keep your pieces coordinated and press on.
Black plays Kh7, the only square. Keep your king safe; h4 was a good, simple plan.
Black plays Rxb2, grabbing a pawn. The game is very hard for you now; keep your king safe and look for checks to trade pieces. Lesson: stay calm in tough spots and make your opponent prove the win.
Black takes your pawn, which is expected. Take it back with your knight next.
Big mistake by black! His bishop move loses a lot. You can win material with Na4, attacking his bishop on c5. Lesson: when your opponent blunders, slow down and hunt for the move that wins a piece.
Black castles to safety. Now both kings are tucked in, so play on the open lines.
Black's queen swings to c5. Watch that diagonal and keep your pieces coordinated.

Black grabs another pawn with his queen — but this was greedy, Qe7 was better. You can play R3d2 to trap and trade off his queen. Lesson: a deep-diving queen can get trapped, so look for moves that box it in.
You put your pawn in the middle to meet White. This is a solid Queen's Pawn opening. Lesson: fighting for the center early is always a good plan.
Your bishop goes to an active square aiming at White's king side. Best spot for it.
You take back with the knight, landing it on an active center square. Good recapture.

You push your pawn forward, but it just gets traded and opens lines for White (about three-quarters of a pawn lost). Better was Qd6, lining your queen up toward White's king. Lesson: don't push a pawn that the enemy can simply swap off.
Bc4! Your bishop attacks White's queen and grabs the upper hand. Exactly the right punch. Lesson: when a piece is attacked and can't escape well, you win material.
You pull the queen back and keep queens on the board. Best choice.
You walk the king to f8 and out of the checks. Good, basically the only move.
Rxe4+! You take the bishop with check and you are completely winning. Lesson: when you're ahead, keep grabbing free pieces with checks. Well played at the finish.
e5! Nice. You strike the center and chase the f4 bishop at the same time. Best move.
Qe7 is loose — it lets their knight take on c7 with check and grab even more. Bb6 was safer. Lesson: with the enemy knight near your king, guard c7 before anything else.
Bxc4 trades bishops. Fine and simple, fewer pieces helps the side that is behind a little.
Rd8 retreats, but it lets their plan roll on. The rook had better squares. You are under real pressure now.
h6 shoos the knight back. Good, simple move.
They take Nxc6. The trade helps you a little; recapture and keep the king active.
They push g4, which lets your king step in. Use Kd6 to head toward their pawns.
They take fxg6. Recapture and keep going.
You played g6 to fianchetto your bishop, a fine setup. The engine liked c5 to fight for the center right away, but g6 is okay.
Well done — you take back the pawn and the material is even again. Your knight sits nicely in the center.
Good — the queen retreats safely to d8. You lose a little time but stay solid.
Good — you take the pawn and keep things solid. Your position is healthy.
The knight to e7 develops but blocks your own pieces a bit. Nf6 was more active and hit the bishop. A small step back.
Good recapture with the rook — at least your rook is active and central. Keep fighting.
Good — the king moves to c7, the right square. Keep finding safe king moves.
You start with the Queen's Pawn opening, pushing the pawn to the center. A calm, solid first move.

You quietly develop the knight, but you missed the gift. Taking exd5 was much stronger and wins material in the center. Lesson: when the enemy queen comes out early, look first for a way to attack it or grab the center.
Your bishop slides to h4 to pin the knight, but d2 for the queen was simpler and stronger.
You castle — well done, your king is finally safe. This was the right moment.
Black's queen comes to f4 to make threats. Stay calm — your knight can come back with check and trade queens.
You take back the pawn on b4. Good — material is even again and you're well placed.
Your rook comes to d1, taking the open file. Good — open files are highways for your rook.
You take the queen on e7 — good, trading into a simpler position where you can defend.
You play f3 to make a shield, but Kh3 was safer. This lets Black's rook come in with check. Lesson: with your king being chased, fewer pawn moves and more safe king steps.
You move the king to h3 — perfect, you slipped out of the checks. Nicely done.
Your queen goes to c7, but Qf4 was needed to defend. This lets Black's attack grow. Lesson: when your king is in danger, bring the queen home to help, not away on a hunt.
Your king goes to e1, the only move. Keep hoping for a way to block.
The opponent puts the bishop on a strong square aiming at your f7. Watch that weak f7 spot, and keep developing.
The opponent develops the last knight and eyes your e5 pawn. Keep an eye on whether e5 is well guarded.
Big gift! The opponent's pawn push just drops a pawn. Take it with axb4 and you come out ahead.
You snap up a pawn with your queen, which is okay. Pushing d5 was a touch sharper, but this is fine.
Your bishop comes out to an active spot. A small note: developing the knight with Nf6 was a touch better, but this is okay.
You recapture with the pawn and open your rook's file. Exactly right.
Your knight leaps into d4. Active, though f6 to chase the bishop was a shade cleaner — still fine.
You play c6, but d5 right away was stronger and freed your game. Lesson: prepare your pawn break, then play it without delay.
You recapture with the pawn, but taking with the bishop (Bxe4) kept you better placed. The pawn grab left your pieces a little tangled.
You missed it — Rg5+ was crushing. Instead Rh5 lets their pawn promote. Lesson: always check for a checking move before quiet moves, it can be winning.
You grab the rook with Bxd1. You're winning easily; Bf3 was fancier, but this wins material too.
Good. Your knight comes out and attacks their e5 pawn right away.
They take your knight. This is the best for them; just recapture and keep going.
Blunder by them — but it helps you! They grab your bishop and you simply take back with fxe3, opening your rook's file.
They move their king to the corner. No threat — keep pressing with your strong pieces.
They connect their rooks, but it's too late. Win the knight: take it with Bxc6.
They push f4 hoping for tricks. Calm move d4 was simplest, but their pawn is weak and easy to win.
Your opponent pushes the other center pawn early. This is a little loose, and now you can just take it.
You play d5 and open up the center. Great — this gives your pieces room and grabs space.
You grab the bishop with your king. Perfect — you are now up a clear piece.
You pin their knight with the bishop, which is okay, but you missed the big shot Bxf2+. Lesson: before a quiet move, always look for a check that wins.
This is the costly mistake of the game. Bf3 walks into Nxf3 and just loses your bishop. Better was Re1+ to check and stay active. Lesson: before moving a piece, check if it can simply be captured.
You play c5, hitting the center pawn from the side. This is fine, but the easy move Nf6 was a touch better because it develops a piece right away.
You play Nc6, developing and eyeing the center. This is the engine's top choice — well done.
You play Bxc2, but this was the wrong piece. Better was e6 to stay solid; with Bxc2 your bishop wanders off and lets Bb4 hit your rook. Tip: count the safety of a piece before it grabs a pawn.
You play Qxc5, winning the knight back. Reasonable, though a6 first kept a touch more. The material is close to even again.
You play e6, but this misses the danger. Kd8 was needed to hide the king. After e6 they play Qb5+ and start grabbing your pawns with check. Tip: when checks are coming, get the king safe first.
You play Kc7, walking the king to safety. Good — this is the top move and keeps everything together.
You play Bc7, blocking the check well. Good — this is the right move and holds your position.
You play Nxd2, winning the bishop. Good — this is the top move and claws back material.
This is the Italian Game. Their bishop now points at your weak f7 square, so keep an eye on it. Lesson: in this opening, always watch f7.
They pin your knight. Not their best, but you can hit their queen now.
Their queen checks and is about to grab your rook in the corner.
They block and offer a queen trade. Not their best.
They castle and link their rooks. Their king is safe now.
They tuck their king into the corner for safety.
Black gets ready to point a bishop along the long line. You can take the center now.
Black castles, tucking his king away. Carry on with your plan.
Black plays Na6, a passive blunder instead of kicking your knight. Punish it with Bf4, which guards your e5 pawn and keeps you on top.
Castling was slow. Better was Be7, which attacks and wins the d6 pawn. Lesson: grab a free target before you tidy up.
g4 was a mistake that loosens your king. Better was b4 to chase the knight and keep your edge. Lesson: don't push pawns near your own king without a reason.
b4 finally kicks the knight. Perfect timing.
You take back with the bishop. Fine.
Bb3 was slightly off; Bb5 hitting the knight was sharper. Minor.
Bc2 is okay; a4 was a touch better.
Bb3 is the right square. Good.
Bb1 keeps the bishop safe. Good.
Black centralizes the king. Carry on.
Black pushes f5. Fine.
Be8 is fine.
Bxe4+ recaptures with check. Good.
Bb7 is Black's best. The bishop now stares down the long line at your middle, so be careful with that pawn road.
Be7 develops Black's bishop quietly. It is a touch slow; you still have time to play d4.
g6 weakens Black's dark squares a little. A strong try here is Qd3, lining your queen up toward the king side.
They point the bishop down the long line. Calm play — just keep building your pieces.
Their knight jumps to the middle. Annoying, but you can chase it with Bd2.
They take your knight too. You must recapture — gxf3 is the move.
Their king steps up to defend. Now keep checking and grabbing — Qxf7 is strong.
They push a pawn on the side. Harmless — you can hit with Bb5.
They defend with the rook. Press on — Rg7 keeps them tied down.
Their king steps the wrong way (Ke8). Now snatch the loose knight with Rxa7! Rxa7.
You swing the rook behind. The best move here.
Walking the king to e3 let their rook check you and slowed you down; Rg7+ was clearly better. Lesson: don't put your king where it can be checked.
You move the king to the corner safely. Good.
The check Ra8+ was fine but Re3 kept more control. Minor inaccuracy.
You start with the most popular first move. You take the center and open paths for your bishop and queen. Great start.
You castle your king to safety too. Smart and important — but Nxe5 winning the pawn was the bigger prize.
You push to challenge black's pawns on the side. A reasonable try, though just a3 kept things calmer.
You ask the black bishop a question with h3. Useful little move to gain space and time.
You capture on f6, breaking up the pawns in front of black's king. Best move and very strong.
This bishop move drifts the wrong way. Rxa5 was free — take the loose pawn! Lesson: grab free pawns before fancy ideas.
This bishop move misses the mark. Bf3 was better, keeping things safe — now black gets counterplay on the g-file. Watch your king.
You put the bishop on f3, a great diagonal pointing at black's king side. Good developing of the attack.
You plant the bishop on d5, a powerful diagonal aiming near black's king. Strong and best.
Black plays c6 to make a little box for the king. It is slow, so just keep building your pieces.
Black takes back with the pawn, dxe5. The center is now open and even. Keep finishing development.
Black plays a6 to get ready to push pawns on the side. You can answer a4 to stop that pawn storm.
Black plays Re8, but this loses time and lets you attack. Jump in with Ng5 to hit f7 and Black's loose setup.
Black takes the knight with the rook, Rxf7. Now follow up to grab back some material.
You recapture with Kxf1, the only good way. Fine — you keep material even.
You play Kg1, stepping the king to safety. Correct — deal with the check calmly.
You play Qf5+, a check, but taking with Rxf7+ first won more. The queen check is less sharp. Lesson: when a trade wins a piece, take it before drifting with checks.
You play Qg3+, but this is a big miss — h4 kept a winning attack. The check lets Black escape and even take over. Lesson: before you check, ask if the king simply walks away and leaves you worse.
You play g3 to make air for your king, but Qb5 was better. This lets Black's queen come in with check. Lesson: make luft when it's calm, not when the enemy queen can pounce.
They bring out the bishop to aim at your weak f7 square. This is the Italian Game. Keep developing and watch f7.
You take the d4 pawn. This is fine, though stepping the bishop back to b6 was a touch better.
You take the bishop with your king. Good, you are now up material.
You slide the queen to g4, a strong active spot. Nicely done.
They check with Qd7+, but this hangs the queen. Take it for free with Bxd7 — you win the whole queen! Lesson: always check if a checking piece can simply be captured.
White develops the other knight to c3. Nothing scary — keep getting your pieces out.
White recaptures with the queen, naturally. Continue developing.
White checks with Ng5+, but it's just a bluff with no follow-up. Simply step the king back.
White grabs the g7 pawn with check pressure. Your king is exposed, so look for a defending move.
You push d4 and now you own a big center. Perfect plan.
Bishop to f4 looks active, but it walks into Bb4 pinning your knight; O-O first was simpler. Lesson: get your king safe before making fancy bishop moves.
Castling is normally great, but here Qe2 was stronger to fight for the center; still, your king is now safe. Lesson: king safety is good, but watch what the enemy queen is doing.
b3 kicks the black queen away and is solid. Well played.
Rook to b1 lines up on the b-file toward the black king. Nice attacking idea.
Qxd2 wins back the rook and leaves you up material. Clean and correct.
Rb2 is too passive; Rf4 to get active was better. Lesson: rooks belong on active files and ranks, not defending from behind. Still even.
Ra1 lets the king win your knight; Nb3 saved it and kept you on top. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, move it to safety before doing anything else. This drops a lot.
They defend the pawn with a knight. Fair play — now you both develop calmly.
They take your pawn. You can win it back — the engine likes Bb5 here, pinning and pressing their knight.
They retreat the bishop. Just develop with Bf4 and finish getting your pieces out.
They center their knight. No problem — you can simply trade it off.
They hold the bishop but allow a strong reply — you can play bxc6+, taking with check! Grab that chance.
They step the king aside. No issue — keep going.
They reposition the queen. Keep your pieces busy.
They race their passed pawn forward. You should take the loose b-pawn with Rxb6 and stay busy.
They give up the rook for your knight. A forced trade — just recapture.
Black defends the pawn with the knight. A solid, expected move.
Black retakes with the knight. Now Qb3 hits both the knight and the weak f7 point at the same time.
Black missed the strong Bxf3. Instead Nb6 lets you off the hook — play Nbd2 and you are fine.
Black blocks with Bd6. You can keep the bishop strong with Bg3, staying a little better.
Black missed the strong Bd5. Instead Raf8 lets you jump in — play Ne4, getting your knight into the game.
Black takes back with the rook. Even trade; now grab the loose bishop with Nxe6.
Black doubles rooks on the second row — dangerous! Block and trade with Ne3 to slow them.
Black doubles rooks again on the second rank. Strong for Black — get your rook back with Rc1 to defend.
Black grabs the a3 pawn. Both sides are racing now; keep your rook busy and aggressive.
Black's king goes back to h7. Keep coordinating your rook and knight together.
Your opponent starts with a side move (g3) to put the bishop on a long line. Take the center while you can.
White finishes the bishop fianchetto; a normal move, no threat.
White's e3 was loose. Strike now with d4 to open lines and gain the edge.
White's Qe2 dropped material. Punish with Bd3! pinning and winning the exchange.
White brings the queen back; a quiet move, no danger.
c6 is a bit slow. Better was Qf6 to get your queen active and press. Lesson: keep your strongest piece busy when you lead.
Queen to b2 gets active and eyes white's weak pawns — good.
h5 is slow. The b3 pawn is still free — Qxb3 was better. Lesson: collect easy pawns first.
You trade rooks on e2 — simplifying is smart when ahead.
Pushing e5 was a mistake — it gives white a chance to break with fxe5. Better was Kf5, marching your king up fast. Lesson: in pawn endings, the king is your strongest piece — move it forward.
King to f3 heads to win white's kingside pawns — good.
You push g4, racing your pawn toward the end — good.
Black pushes e5 and takes the center too. This is normal and fair.
Black plays Be7, another slip. dxe5 wins the e5 pawn cleanly right now.
Black recaptures with Kxd8. You are way ahead in material now — stay calm and trade pieces.
Black checks with Bb4+. Block calmly with c3 to push the bishop back.
Black plays hxg5 and wins your bishop. You are now far behind.
Black plays Nxg4+ and wins your queen with check. A painful loss; keep your queen guarded next time.
Black plays Bxa3, a small mistake but Black is still winning. Stay calm and make them prove it.
Lucky break — your opponent did not take your loose bishop and played a slow pawn move instead. Take their bishop now with Bxa6 and stay ahead.
