You grab the pawn with Nxh3+, which wins material, though Qd3 trading queens was even cleaner. Lesson: when far ahead, trading queens makes the win simple and safe.
You invade with Qd1 — the engine's top move. Great, your queen is deep in his camp.
You snatch the b2 pawn — fine and safe, you keep rolling forward. Good, more material in the bank.
You take the knight with your king, winning material — engine's top move. Great, the trades favor you hugely.
Your king walks up the board, which is fine in this winning spot. Keep it safe and march your passed pawns.
Checkmate! You bring the queen to h1 and end the game. Well played finishing it cleanly — you spotted the mate when it counted.
You play c6 to make a safe home for your queen. Solid and sensible.
You play Nd7 to bring out a knight. Fine; Nf6 was just a hair more natural.
You recapture with Qxf6, keeping your queen active in the center.
You castle long with O-O-O, tucking your king away and bringing a rook to the center. Sound.
You play Rf5 — now you found it, eyeing the weak f3 pawn. Good.
You play Rg8, taking the open g-file with your rook. Good plan.
You play Rd4 — exactly right, the rook is safe and still active.
Great — you take your share of the center right away. This is the engine's top choice.
You develop the bishop, but b6 was stronger — it attacks the loose c5 pawn. Lesson: when a pawn pokes out and looks weak, gang up on it.
You castle and tuck your king away safely. Best move.
You scoop up the knight with the queen. You are up material now — best move.
White offers to trade bishops and hits your bishop. Just trade them off.
White develops a rook to the center. Watch his rooks and keep your pieces coordinated.
White's queen retreats. Keep your pieces busy and look for tricks.
White's rook comes to e2 to challenge yours. Stay active.
Black copies you and meets in the center. Now you can grab space by developing your knight to attack their pawn.
Black pins your knight to your queen with the bishop. Now push it away with h3 to ask the bishop a question.
You play the check Qb5+, perfectly using the blunder. The pawn and knight are about to fall.
Black tucks the king to h8. Now d4 hits the center and your pieces come alive.
Black takes back with the rook. You are still well ahead; bring your knight to a strong square.
Black brings the knight to f7 to defend. You are still up material — trade off with Nxc5 to simplify.
You take on g6 with check, removing a dangerous bishop. Good defensive trade.
You give the check Ra7+, exactly right. Black is squeezed and you stay in full control.
Nf6 develops your knight and pokes at White's e4 pawn. Nice — this is exactly the engine's top choice.
d5 looks active but it gives White an easy trade and loosens your center; c6 first was steadier. Lesson: don't push a pawn into the center if it just opens lines for the other side.
Nc6 develops your last minor piece. Good, simple play.
Qd5 centralizes the queen, though Bf5 to develop with tempo was a bit sharper. A small inaccuracy, not a real error.
Qh5 defends the bishop and keeps your queen active. The engine agrees.
Qxf5 takes back. Fine, though recapturing with the rook kept a touch more pressure.
Nxd2 wins White's queen back, easing the damage from move 48. Good recovery.
Kh7 is a slow king move; keeping the rook active with Rf5 was better. Lesson: in rook endings, activity usually beats slow shuffling.
Ra5 keeps your rook active on the open file. A reasonable move.
Kh6 brings your king toward the action. Good — active kings are key in endgames.
You support your e4 pawn with d3. Solid, but Nc3 developed a piece faster. Lesson: try to move a new piece each turn in the opening.
Their queen grabs your c4 pawn. It is just one pawn — keep developing with your knight and you are okay.
Knight to b5! The best move. It attacks near their king and the weak c7 square.
They play f6 to chase your queen, but this opens their king to a check. Qe6+ jumps in with a strong check.
You recapture on f5 with your pawn. Clean and good.
Nb5+! The best move. Your knight checks and pushes the king into the open center.
Qc7#! Checkmate! Well played — your queenside attack paid off. Lesson: open lines toward the enemy king and keep checking until mate.
h6 is slow and wastes time; it does nothing for development. Better was Nf6 to develop and guard the king side. Lesson: in the opening, move pieces out, not edge pawns.
Bb4 pins nothing useful and ignores your king; d5 was better to hit their center and free your game. Lesson: when behind, fix king safety first.
You moved your pawn one square. Pushing it two squares with e4 grabs more of the center, but this is still a fine, safe start.
You develop the bishop and pin Black's knight. Be2 was a touch simpler, but this is okay.
You ask the bishop a question with h3 — move or trade. This is the right idea.
You put your rook on the open d-file, which is good. Pushing e4 was even stronger here.
You start with the king pawn going two squares. This grabs the center — a great first move.
You place the bishop on an active line toward Black's king. The e5 pawn push was even stronger.
You take the pawn. Correct — best move.
You jump the knight in to bother the queen. Active and fine.
You snap up the queen! Best move — you win huge material.
You reposition the bishop. Pushing your passed a-pawn was a bit stronger. Lesson: an extra passed pawn wants to run.
You take f7 with the knight, best move — your knights swarm Black's king.
You give the check, starting the mating net. Best move — the king must run.
You bring the knight to c6 to develop. Almost equal to the engine's e5 — a fine, normal move.
White's queen goes to b3. The engine liked Bf5 here, but your plan is still good.
White plays h3 to kick your knight. Your knight on f2 can grab the rook in the corner with Nxh1.
You play Bc5, but castling with O-O-O was much safer and better. Lesson: when you can castle to safety, usually do it.
You play b5, which weakens the squares near your own king — Qd7 was much safer. Lesson: be careful pushing pawns in front of your own king.
You play Qg6 to get active. Qd3 was a little stronger, but this is okay.
You play Qc4, but Qg6 was better and kept your queen more useful.
You play Kc7, but Bc7 was a little better. Still fine.
White plays Be4 to get active. Keep your rook busy behind passed pawns.
White plays Nf4 instead of the stronger Nd5+. Push your h-pawn — it's dangerous.
White gives Ne6+, check. Step your king to the safe side (b6 is best).
White plays Be4, a blunder. Take the knight with gxf3 — you win a piece.
White plays Bc6. Keep your rook hunting White's weak pawns.
White's king goes to c3. Bring your king up to help your pawns.
White plays Kc4 to stay near the action. You're winning — keep your king and rook working together to round up the knight.
You bring out the knight. Good and natural.
You castle. Good — your king is safe now.
The bishop eyes your knight, but it is no real danger; h6 can ask it a question.
The king steps aside. Now bring your queen back to safety.
White gives a rook for the bishop, then wins your knight with e5 — a clever trade for him. Take the rook back.
White lifts the rook to attack. Meet it with Re6 to defend along the rank.
White grabs the h7 pawn. Keep developing — Nd7 still hits the bishop.
White trades queens, which helps you simplify. Take back with the king.
White offers a rook trade on the b-file. Trading is fine for you.
You develop your other knight to c3. A fine move, but you missed the free pawn: Nxe5 wins it because Black left e5 unguarded.
You retreat to b3, but this lets Black push c4 and trap the knight idea. The check Bb5+ first was much better and kept Black tangled up.
Black takes back with dxe3. Now bring a piece out — Nc3 develops and keeps your advantage.
Black moves the queen to c5, eyeing your pawns. Defend simply; your queen can come to f3 with good play.
Black plays g6, a slow move that helps you. Get your bishop out with Be2 and rush to castle your king to safety.
White takes your pawn; grab it right back so material stays even.
White castles to safety; carry on developing and plan to castle yourself.
White takes back and now owns two bishops aimed at your side; castle soon.
White trades bishops; take back with the pawn to keep your structure whole.
White brings a rook to the open file; match it and get your own rooks active.
White trades rooks; take back and keep your last rook active.
White checks again; step your king to a calm square.
White opens with the king's pawn to take the center. This is the most common first move. Just develop your pieces calmly.
Another slow pawn move by White. Grab space in the center with d5 while you can.
Big blunder by White! Pushing f4 leaves the e4 pawn loose — you can win it with Nxe4 right now.
White blunders by taking on b6. Take back with Qxb6 — your queen comes out with power.
You push to take more center. The engine slightly liked c3 to support it first, but this is fine and natural.
You develop the knight to c3. The engine saw e5 as a strong push here, but Nc3 is a solid developing move. No harm.
You shift the queen to b4. This is fine and roughly equal to the engine's Qb3. No problem at all.
You take the rook! You are now winning a whole rook. Fantastic — just stay calm and trade pieces when you can.
Careful! b3 dropped your c2 pawn. c3 was safe. After this Black grabs c2 with the rook. Lesson: before a quiet pawn move, check what it leaves undefended.
You check again with Qa4+. The engine preferred Qd1, but this is still equal-ish and keeps Black uncomfortable. Okay.
Black pushes a5 to support his b-pawn. You can play a3 to challenge it. Keep things controlled.
Black activates his rook on b2. Watch your b3 pawn but stay calm — your two rooks dominate. Centralize and push.
Black checks with Rb1+. Just step the king to h2 — the check leads nowhere for him. Easy.
Black queens with check, but it's a trick that fails. Take the new queen: Rxb1 wins it for free. Easy finish.
Nice — your knight comes to a strong square and gets you ready to castle. This is the engine's top choice.
You keep the pin by retreating to h4 — exactly the engine's choice. Well played.

You took with the bishop (Bxf6), which throws away most of your edge. exf6 was much stronger — it wins the knight and keeps a big lead. Lesson: when two captures are possible, check which one wins more.
Your opponent checks you with Qd4+. Just step your king to h1 — calm and safe.
Your opponent grabs your f4 pawn with the queen. Bring your knight to d5 — it is active and helps your attack.
Your opponent copies you. This is fine — now you can develop your pieces and fight for the center.
They develop their knight. Calm move — continue getting your pieces out.
They tuck their king away on the queenside. Note where their king is — your attack later should aim there.
They push the pawn forward. Stay calm and look for ways to attack the bishop and that pawn.
Their knight jumps to a central square. Watch it — meet it by getting your queen active with Qb3.
This drops material to Bxf2+. Kh1 was safe. Lesson: when checked, move the king to a safe square before giving up a piece.
King goes the wrong way and loses the bishop. Kg1 was safe. Lesson: in a check, pick the square that keeps your pieces protected.
Kb2 was better, but the queen is lost anyway.
You bring the rook back to defend and stay active. Fine.
Re5 was better, keeping the rook active. In these endings, an active rook is your best friend.

Careful — Bxf7+ looks scary but it does not work and gives away your good bishop. The simple Nxd4 just won you a piece, because Black's knight was not protected. Lesson: count the pieces before you sacrifice; only give up material if you truly win it back.
Black tucks the king to e8. Keep developing and use your lead in piece activity.
Black plays h6 to ask your bishop a question. Decide where the bishop goes.
Black moves the queen to g7 to stay safe. Now finish your development and open lines.
Perfect — Qxc6+ checks the king and wins the knight. You are storming back into the game.
Rh5 is still strong and keeps you totally winning, but Qd7 would have finished things faster. Lesson: when several moves win, pick the one that goes straight for the king.
Your opponent opens with the king's pawn. A normal start — just get ready to fight for the center.
Your bishop comes to f5, but it does little here. Nc6 to keep developing was better.
You play the active Bg4 instead. Not the most, but a fine move.
Your knight comes to d7. Solid, but castling first was a bit safer.
Mistake — Bf5 lets their knight come to e5. Pushing c4 was much stronger, gaining space and bothering their pieces.
You take the bishop with bxc4. Now you have the piece back and stand better.
You retreat the rook to d8. Safe and sound.
Your bishop comes to e4, aiming at their pieces. Reasonable.
Mistake — Ba6 lets their knight come to f5 with annoying ideas. Be4 kept your bishop powerful in the middle.
You bring a rook to c2 to fight the runner. It holds, but moving your king to g7 was the clean choice.
You recapture on c2. Good, your rook is still deep in their camp.
You check with Rxg2+. Strong — your rook keeps making threats.
Their king heads over to stop your pawn. Keep pushing — a4 marches on.
Now you push e4 and build a big wall of pawns in the center. Nice idea. The engine slightly likes Nf3 first, but your move is fine.
Black plays a6, getting ready to push pawns on the side. Calm move — carry on with your plan in the center.
Black recaptures with the queen on d5, a strong central post. Watch that this active queen doesn't start grabbing your pawns.
Black's queen comes to e6. Keep an eye on your h3 pawn near your king and defend if needed.
Black plays Bxe5 and wins your center pawn. This hurts, but stay focused and look for the best way to fight back.
You start with the king pawn going two squares. This is a great first move — it grabs the center and opens lines for your queen and bishop.
They bring a knight to c6. A small slip by them. You can answer by playing d4 to take the big center.
They play e6 to free their dark bishop. A normal, solid move. Just keep developing your pieces.
They take back with the g-pawn, but this badly breaks the shield around their king. This is a big blunder. Punish it now with Knight to e4, heading straight for the weak king.
They play Re8, but it cannot stop your attack. Keep going.
You start with the king's pawn going to the middle. Great first move — it grabs the center and opens lines for your pieces.
Black develops a knight to c6. Just keep your plan and finish bringing pieces out.
You play d3, but a4 was much better to attack the b5 pawn. Lesson: when the enemy pushes pawns on the side, strike at them fast.
You recapture with the knight. Strong piece in the middle — good job.
Queen to d2 connects your pieces. Reasonable; a rook to e1 was also good.
Ng3 is a big blunder — it lets Black win your bishop with check. Bd1 saves the bishop instead. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, move it to safety before anything else.
You start with the king pawn going to e4. A strong, normal first move that opens lines for your pieces.
d4 builds a big strong center with two pawns. Exactly the right plan. Well done.
Queen to f4 is the right move, getting out of the attack. Good save.
Black plays Rfc8 to attack your queen on c7. The strong reply is Nc3, developing with threats against the d5 knight.
Bd6 develops your bishop to a good square aiming at the kingside. A fine, simple developing move.
Qc6 keeps your queen active and defends d5; a reasonable choice, though Qf7 was a touch tidier.
You start with the classic king-pawn opening. Good first move that grabs the center.
Black pins your knight with Bb4. It is annoying but not scary. You can break the pin later with a3.
You play f3 and kick the bishop. Strong move that wins time.
Black recaptures with the pawn. The position is calm; now build a plan with your queen and rooks.
Black plays Nc4 and wins your bishop, just as the trouble showed. From here, save what you can — try fxg5 to grab a pawn back and keep fighting.
You developed your knight, but c5 was stronger to hit White's center right away. The center is getting big and needs to be challenged. Lesson: break a big center with a pawn before it gets strong.
Good — you block the check with a solid pawn and keep your position strong.
Great — your queen steps back safely and now aims at White's weak d3 pawn.

This knight jump looks scary but it loses a lot of value; Be4, keeping everything solid, was much better. You got lucky that White did not punish it. Lesson: before a fancy jump, check that your piece won't get into trouble.
Your queen drifts to the side; Qc4 was better to offer a trade while you are ahead. Trading helps the side with more material. Lesson: when ahead, swapping pieces makes winning easier.
You try to break White's center, but Qc4 was stronger and more active. Lesson: an active queen in the center is powerful.
Both rooks went passive; Qc4 was far more active. When you can attack, don't curl up. Lesson: in a good spot, keep making threats instead of retreating.
Walking the king up runs into trouble and loses your rook; Qxf1+ to trade was the way to fight on. Lesson: when checked in danger, trading pieces is often the safest choice.
They develop a knight. Notice you could pin it with your bishop later.
Their knight jumps to a strong central square and eyes your bishop. Be ready to challenge it.
They push the pawn to cramp you. Bring your knight to d7 to get organized.
They swing the rook across to the center. Stay alert for a pawn break.
They develop their bishop to the long diagonal.
They take your knight. Take back.
Their king attacks your knight. The strong reply is the e5 pawn push.
They offer a rook trade. Trading is fine.
They grab your b-pawn. Keep racing your own passed pawn.
They recapture. The race is on.
They keep pushing their passer. Watch the race carefully.
They make a new queen. This is tough now — push your pawn and dodge checks.
They take your e-pawn. Now you are fighting for a draw at best.
Huge mistake by them — this check lets you queen! Play Kf2 and your pawn promotes next move.
They check instead of setting up the mate. Stay alert.
You answer with the Sicilian Defense. This is a strong, fighting reply for black — well done.
You open a path for your bishop and build a solid pawn wall. A good, calm move.
Your queen comes out to an active square. Roughly equal — a fine choice.
This drops a pawn to a bishop check. Bf8 first was safer; now Bb5+ hits you. Lesson: before pushing a pawn, check for enemy checks it opens up.
You poke his bishop with the pawn. A reasonable little move.
Your queen steps back to a safe square. Close to best — fine.
You drop the bishop back to a good square. Top choice — well done.
This rook move drops a lot — Qb7 to trade queens was much better and calmer. Lesson: when behind or under pressure, trading queens makes defense easier.
You play e4. Great start — this opens lines for your pieces and grabs the center.
Nxd4 recaptures nicely. Your knight sits strong in the middle.
Ne2 is passive and unpins, but it's a step back. Qf3 was more active, eyeing the kingside. Lesson: try to keep pieces forward, not retreating.
Nc7 jumps in but it's loose — it doesn't really threaten enough. Qb3 was stronger, keeping pressure. Lesson: a knight deep in enemy land needs a real target, not just a 'looks scary' square.
Kf1 steps the king aside — this was actually the right reply to stay safe.
Qf3 is a strange early queen move. It blocks your opponent's own knight and wastes time. You don't need to fear it — just keep developing.
Be6 develops your bishop to a nice spot. Solid, though d5 first was even sharper.
Castling long puts your king on the queenside, but g6 first was simpler. Your king is a little airy here, so play carefully.
c4 pushes a pawn but loosens things. Be7 first, finishing development, was cleaner. Don't rush pawn moves before your pieces are out.
Bxf2+ wins one pawn back but trades off your strong bishop. h5 was steadier. After this you are still behind.
Bxc4 recaptures the knight. Fair trade; keep trying to stay active.
Rxe4 wins the e4 pawn back. Well spotted — keep the rook busy.
Kc7 calmly answers the check. Exactly right.
Rxa2 grabs a pawn but lets their rook check and grab your b7 pawn. b6 first, keeping things solid, was safer. Count what your opponent gets back before you grab.
Ree2 doubles your rooks on the second rank. Good — together they are strong.
Rxb4 wins another pawn. Nice — your rooks are doing great work now.
Rcc2 doubles your rooks on the second rank again. Great — this is the dream setup in rook endings.
b5 starts your passed pawn rolling. Good — but bringing the king with Kc7 was even quicker.
b3 keeps your pawn racing. Good — it's almost home.
Qb2+ keeps checking. Fine — but try to line up checks that also stop their h-pawn from queening.
Qf5+ checks. Good — keep driving the king while watching the h-pawn.
Qg6+ checks again. You're slowly squeezing the king toward the edge.
Qe5+ checks again. Good control — add your king to the attack.
Qg6+ checks the king. Good — drive it back toward the corner.
Your bishop comes out and aims at the enemy knight. A fine developing move; later your big plan is to grab the center with d4.
The queen on d3 sits in an awkward spot and drops some advantage. Better was Ne2: it keeps your pieces tidy and avoids letting them mess up your pawns.
You take back with the bishop. Taking with the queen was a touch better to keep your pawns together, but this is okay.
Your queen swings over to b7 to go pawn hunting. The c7 pawn is your target.
The queen jump to e5 lets them get tricky with Rxc3. Better was Qb7, keeping everything safe and defended.
Your bishop shifts to b4. A fine move, very close to the engine's choice.
Their king must step to h8. Forced, as expected.
You bring out your knight and attack the black pawn in the center. Good, normal development.
You trade knights. It works, but the sharp Bxf7+ first was even stronger, hitting the king. Lesson: look for checks that hit the king before quiet trades.
You castle and get your king safe. Smart and simple.

This loses material. Pushing b4 opens the long dark diagonal straight to your rook in the corner. After Bxb4 cxb4 Black plays Qxa1 and wins your rook. Nd2 was safe. Lesson: before a pawn move, check what diagonals or lines it opens toward your own pieces.
You develop the bishop and bump the queen. This is close to best, nothing to worry about.
You snap up the c6 pawn for free. Nicely done — you win back material.
You recapture with the bishop, getting back onto the strong diagonal. Best move; make the most of what you have.
You center the rook. Reasonable, though bxa5 winning the pawn was still on offer.
White opens with the king pawn. You answer with the Sicilian, a strong fighting setup for black.
White trades pawns with exd5. Just take back so your center stays solid.
White plays a4 to attack your b5 pawn. You need to deal with this; pushing b4 keeps your pawns strong and chases the knight.

Your knight to c6 also blocks your c-pawn. A small slip — Nf6 was tidier because it helps guard your center and gets ready to castle. Lesson: in these openings, the f6 square is usually the best home for this knight.
You check and trade knights. This is fine, very close to equal, so no worries about it.
White takes your knight with check. Normal — just recapture and your queen gets active.
White brings out a knight to a good square. Nothing scary yet.
You take back. You are a clean pawn ahead now.
You take back with the queen. Good.
You develop your bishop. Okay, but d5 in the center was the stronger plan.
You push e5, which weakens your own squares and lets White's knight target them. d5 was stronger and safer. Lesson: don't push pawns that leave holes behind.
Forced — the only move.
Bringing the queen out this early is risky. Nf3 was better — it develops a piece and the queen can get chased around later. Lesson: develop knights and bishops first, save the queen for later.
Excellent. You strike in the center with d4 and challenge their pawns.
Well done. The rook lands on the open d-file and presses their position.
Your knight comes out to a good square and guards the center. Solid developing move.
You took with dxc5, but this lets Black grab your b2 pawn. The quiet knight to c3 was better, keeping things safe. Lesson: before a capture, check what your opponent can grab back.
Black takes back the pawn on c5. Now your bishop can recapture and you regain material — take it.
Black plays Kg7 to support the kingside and unpin. Normal — just keep building your plan and look at the knight to c4.
Black recaptures on g5 with the pawn, as expected. Now take that pawn back with your bishop to limit the damage.
Black plays Qd7, connecting and preparing to attack. Stay alert on the b7 bishop and the long diagonal toward your king.
Queen to e3 was a costly mistake — it lets Black check and win material with Qxg4+. Playing h3 to cover g4 was needed. Lesson: always check what checks your opponent has before moving.

Rook to f1 was a blunder that loses the game — it walks into a winning attack. The knight to a1, regrouping, was needed. Lesson: when defending, check that your move doesn't open new lines to your king.
You finally play Nf3. Excellent — this is the best move, getting a piece out and guarding your king's side.
You develop the bishop to e3. Not bad, but Nc3 to bring the last knight out was the better builder.
You take the a6 pawn with the queen — the best move, winning the pawn back and staying active.
You jump the knight to d5, a strong central post. Nice and active.
You retreat the knight to g2. Again Qxc7 was better and grabs the pawn. Don't keep passing up the free pawn.
You take the c7 pawn with the queen, but this lets Black hit back; f4 first was stronger. Be careful grabbing pawns when your own king side is loose.
You recapture with Qxe7 — best move, you are clearly ahead.
You push g4, missing the strong Re7. The rook on the 7th rank was crushing; g4 lets Black escape. Lesson: look for active rook moves before pushing pawns.
You push f6 instead of taking the g5 pawn. Rxg5 was better to kill Black's dangerous pawn. Lesson: stop the enemy passed pawn before it runs.
You play Re6+ check — best move, driving the king back.
You play Ke2 to guard. Good, you are keeping the black pawn locked.
You play Ke2 — best move, calmly blocking.
You push a5. A small slip — keeping the king active with Kd2 was a touch faster, but the pawns still win.
Your opponent starts with e3. This is a quiet, slow move that does not grab much of the center. You have time to play in the middle.
Qe2 puts the queen out early. Not the best, but no harm to you yet.
Nf3 brings his knight back. No threat to you. Keep developing.
Ke1 just steps the king over. Your knight is still busy in his camp.
Qe5 centralizes again. Just chase or ignore and develop.
Qxd5 grabs your center pawn. You are still ahead, just keep your pieces working together.
Rxb7 takes your pawn and attacks your bishop. Defend it — Be6 keeps everything protected.
Qxd3 takes your knight. Pieces are trading off.
Nxa7 takes your pawn, but it walks the knight away into the corner — a blunder. Bring your rook in with Rb2 to attack.
Ke4 marches the king up. Bold, but you can keep checking.
Kb5 dodges. Stay with the checks.
Qb6 blocks with the queen. Watch for a trade.
Kb7 steps over. Keep going.
Qc6 offers a queen trade. Be careful — trading helps him here.
You start with the king pawn going to e4. Great first move that opens lines for your pieces.
Bishop to c4 aims at the f7 square near their king. A normal, useful developing move.
Nc3 develops, but again d4 was the strong central break. Remember: pawns in the middle give your pieces room.
Nxf7+ is the right shot, winning the rook with check. Excellent, you spotted the fork and won material back.
Rf1 puts your rook on the open file toward their king. A good, active rook move.
Be3 keeps the position solid and equal-ish for your side. Fine move while you slowly untangle.
c4 gains space but Bd4 was a bit better, centralizing the bishop. Still a fine pawn push.
Bd4 is the best move, putting the bishop on a powerful square. Nicely done, you are pressing on their pieces.
White plays a slow pawn move and gives away a little — this lets you take the center. Play e5 to build a big pawn wall in the middle.
White props up his center. Quiet move; keep building your position.
White's queen escapes your knight. Calm now; a move like c6 keeps everything solid.
White recaptures and his bishop is now active in the middle. Bring a rook to the open file with Rc8.
White takes your knight back, an even trade. Now collect the loose pawn with Qxd3.
White grabs a pawn but it is risky and loses ground. Win the c6 pawn back with Qxc6.
White's knight jumps to a strong central square. Challenge it by offering a queen trade with Ra8.
White attacks your e5 pawn. You can castle (O-O) and stay safe.
White hops the knight to the side. You can trade it off with Bxb5.
You play d5, the Scandinavian. It hits the center right away. A small note: c5 was a touch better, but d5 is a fine, fighting choice for your level.
You develop with Nc6, putting pressure on the d4 pawn. It is fine, though the pawn push c5 was even stronger to attack the center.
You play Nxe3, winning the bishop. Excellent — this is the best move and you grab material.
You castle long, O-O-O, the best move. Your king is now safe and your rook joins the game. Well done.
You play Bd6, eyeing White's king, but Qd5 was stronger to hit more targets at once. Your bishop does point at a nice diagonal though.
You recapture with Rxf8, the best move. Trades are okay here and your rook stays active on the open file.
You play Be5, a good active bishop move. The bishop controls key squares and helps fight White's pawn.
You play Rg1+, giving a check to bother the king — the best move here. Good idea to use checks to gain time.
You play Rg1+, a fine check, though grabbing the h-pawn right away with Rxh4+ was just as strong. Your rook keeps the king busy.

Knight to c3 — perfect. You develop a piece AND attack their queen at the same time, so they must move it again.

Qh6 — superb! Your queen joins the attack right next to their king. The threats are getting deadly.

g5 pushes past instead of trading, leaving more holes near his king. Calmly develop with Be6 and aim at those weak squares.

King to g8, the safe square. Forced and correct.

O-O-O! Good — your king finally finds a home and your rook joins the game.

Excellent — your queen takes the knight and sits on a strong active square. You are doing great here.

The bishop to d5 tries to block, but White is already much better. The engine preferred putting both rooks active. Things are slipping.
Rd1 puts the rook deep but allows Qb5+ check and trouble. The engine wanted R5d7 to defend. Lesson: when your king is open, defend first before attacking.
Good — king to b8 again, holding firm. You are defending the checks well.

White's king steps to e2. Just keep harassing with your active rook.

Small mistake. The knight jumps at f7 but it gets chased away and wastes time. Better was d3, keeping your strong bishop and a solid setup. Lesson: don't attack early if the attack can be kicked back.
A bit slow. Better was d4, hitting their bishop and opening lines for you. The rook move just waits. Lesson: meet a pawn push by striking the center yourself.
Excellent! You snap up the queen. This is a winning material lead — now play safe and simple.
